title: ‘Big Break’ Review: Comedy Quartet Meets Serial-Killer Peril in an Amusing, Tongue-in-Cheek Thriller
description: NYC-based sketch comedy quartet Simple Town, who have performed live and in online shorts over the last decade, make an amusing leap to the feature-
body:
NYC-based sketch comedy quartet Simple Town, who have performed live and in online shorts over the last decade, make an amusing leap to the feature-film format in “Big Break.” Ostensibly playing themselves, the group here gathers at a country manse to celebrate one member’s breakaway mainstream success — and for the other three to beg/cajole him into sharing that good fortune. Unbeknownst to the visitors, there’s an unhappy fifth party already in the house… and more than one homicidal maniac even within that small populace. 
	

	As in their prior work, the troupe’s humor is less a matter of sight gags or punchlines than a well-oiled ensemble dynamic that sends up Gen Y self-absorption, social awkwardness and passive-aggressive competition. It’s not a formula that generates huge laughs, and the material here is seldom all that inspired even as it playfully exploits horror conventions. Yet the results are fun and reasonably funny throughout, with astutely self-deprecating cast turns lent a modest but polished, fast-paced showcase in director Ian Faria’s feature debut.


	Reuniting with long-incommunicado former collaborator Sam (Sam Lanier) is a very big deal to Caro (Caroline Yost), Felipe (Felipe Di Poi) and Will (Will Niedemann), as their neurotically argumentative drive to see him underlines. They must pretend they’re simply glad to spend the weekend at their good buddy’s pad, a sizable estate two hours outside Manhattan, since he’s finally invited them over. But they’re each none-too-quietly seething with covetous anxiety and resentment, particularly since the thing that skyrocketed Sam to Hollywood wealth and fame — writing an animated film called “The Gummy Bear Movie” — happens to contain a lot of lines and ideas that were once group property, used without attribution. The three are desperate to arm-twist their way into a slice of that future-career pie, though they can’t agree on how to broach the subject. No one is pleased when Will, having drunk too much alcohol way too fast, is first to blurt out a request-slash-demand.
	

	But then there’s another issue going on, which at first only the viewer is privy to: Success has gone to Sam’s head in more ways than one, unleashing an inner serial killer whose latest victim (Jefferson White from “Yellowstone”) gets introduced in a classic doomed-hiker-fleeing-through-the-woods sequence. Naturally, there’s a sort of torture dungeon on the premises, which for the time being his guests are mercifully unaware of. But they soon get wise, and in the meantime a captive gets loose. He has very good reason to desire bloody revenge, though some spotty eavesdropping gives him the false impression that everybody here is complicit in the host’s crimes. Soon, they’re all in an armed panic, likely to commit grievous bodily harm deliberately or otherwise.

	While Lanier gets sole screenplay credit, one suspects much improvisational input at work here from the practiced way the leads play off each other. Their air of slightly absurd quasi-spontaneity is nicely amplified by the jittery yet unobtrusive rhythms of the direction and Yost’s editing. Amidst other solid contributions to a resourcefully produced whole, Alt-metal gods Helmet’s 1992 single “Get It” provides the perfect closing-credits sendoff.

schema.headline: ‘Big Break’ Review: Comedy Quartet Meets Serial-Killer Peril in an Amusing, Tongue-in-Cheek Thriller

title: Venice Days Competition Title ‘The Indies’ Boarded by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Barcelona-based world sales company MoreThan Films has acquired period road movie “Les Indes” (“The Indies”), co-written and directed by first-time
body:
Barcelona-based world sales company MoreThan Films has acquired period road movie “Les Indes” (“The Indies”), co-written and directed by first-time feature filmmakers Pauline Julier and Nicolas Chapoulier, ahead of its premiere in the Venice Film Festival’s Giornate Degli Autori (Venice Days).

	Produced by Spain’s Lastor Media (“Alcarràs”) and Switzerland’s Alina Film (“The Currents”) and inspired by true events, “Les Indes” centers on Alejandro (Théo Urtubey), a young Spanish nobleman, who, along with two French soldiers (played by Raphaël Thiéry and Lazare Minoungou), is tasked with delivering a portrait of the infanta of Spain –  Maria Theresa, daughter of King Philip IV – to the young king of France, Louis XIV, in the hope of sealing a fragile alliance between the two countries in 1652.
	

	Set against a backdrop of turbulent transition as the Middle Ages moves into modernity, the film follows the three men on their long and arduous journey, across a Europe ravaged by wars and uprisings, to Versailles. 


	“It is the 17th century: the medieval era is fading in the face of the rise of science, rationalism, and commerce,” Julier and Chapoulier explained in a statement. “The world is no longer merely to be explored – it is to be conquered. Galileo opens new horizons, while mercantilism lays the foundations of capitalism. In this context, popular uprisings erupt under the pressure of taxation and poverty. It is along these roads, marked by tensions between the old world and the new order, that ‘Les Indes’ unfolds.”
	

	“‘Les Indes’ captivated us with its ability to transform a historical episode into a deeply contemporary reflection on power, images, and our relationship with the natural world,” said Queralt Pons Serra, managing partner of MoreThan Films.

	“Rather than simply reconstructing the past, the film uses history as a lens through which to examine the origins of the world we inhabit today. With its bold visual language and meditative storytelling, Pauline Julier and Nicolas Chapoulier have crafted a singular cinematic journey, a singular work that challenges, rewards, and stays with you long after the screening, making it a natural addition to our program.”

	Lidia Damatto, fellow managing partner at MoreThan Films, added: “‘Les Indes’ marks our second collaboration with Alina Film. We worked together on the Locarno breakout hit ‘Hanami’ in 2024, directed by Denise Fernandes and produced by Eugenia Mumenthaler and David Epiney.

	“We’re very happy to continue to work with producers who not only consistently deliver fantastic projects, every year, but who also share our collaborative working philosophy and market approach for arthouse films.”

	The film, which was presented as a work in progress at this year’s ECAM Forum co-production market in Madrid, was recently picked up by Switzerland’s Sister Distribution.

schema.headline: Venice Days Competition Title ‘The Indies’ Boarded by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE)

title: BLacklight, Dark Star Set Wes Miller’s Courtroom Thriller ‘Wildcards’ for Theatrical Tour With Post-Screening Talks
description: BLacklight and Dark Star Pictures have teamed for the nationwide theatrical release of “Wildcards,” creating a unique theatrical experience that the
body: BLacklight and Dark Star Pictures have teamed for the nationwide theatrical release of “Wildcards,” creating a unique theatrical experience that the creatives behind the film hope will spark conversation, community discourse and, of course, box office.The latest feature from writer-director Wes Miller (“Black Heat,” “Call Her King”), “Wildcards” follows the trial of Theodore Sterling, a privileged young man accused of sexually assaulting a young Black woman. As jurors from different backgrounds clash over the evidence, tensions escalate between determined state prosecutor James Jones and veteran defense attorney Greg Sims. The case takes a turn with the arrival of a mysterious “wildcard” witness who claims to know the truth about the night in question. Her connection to the accused raises unsettling questions of bias, credibility and justice.BLacklight and Dark Star Pictures are using the Aug. 27 release date to reimagine a theatrical rollout by pairing a screening in select markets with a moderated discussion featuring members of the cast and creative team, and in some cities, local community leaders, artists and cultural voices.Each tour stop is designed to be a shared cultural event, with organizers calling it an “evening of storytelling, reflection and audience engagement that extends beyond the final credits.”The film’s ensemble cast includes Leon, Elise Neal, Aries Spears, Stakiah Lynn Washington, Crew Morrow, Courtney Grace, Samantha Walkes and Robert Catrini.“I’m excited to bring this film and share the stellar performances of the cast. ‘Wildcards’ represents everything I’m passionate about as a filmmaker — creating authentic and meaningful genre entertainment for the culture,” said Miller. “For me, this theatrical tour is about taking that directly to our communities, city-by-city, and creating the kind of theatrical experience that reminds people why cinema matters.”Producer Andrew van den Houten added: “We are thrilled to continue BLacklight’s distribution partnership with Dark Star Pictures. As BLacklight’s reach expands, bringing writer/director Wes Miller, Leon, and other special guests to national event screenings allows us to deliver a celebratory, unforgettable cinematic experience while connecting deeply with our growing audience.”

schema.headline: BLacklight, Dark Star Set Wes Miller’s Courtroom Thriller ‘Wildcards’ for Theatrical Tour With Post-Screening Talks

title: ‘Your Friends & Neighbors’ Star Lena Hall Joins Chad Michael Murray in ‘Disconnecting Peter’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Tony Award winner Lena Hall has boarded “Disconnecting Peter,” joining previously announced star Chad Michael Murray in the upcoming family drama. T
body:
Tony Award winner Lena Hall has boarded “Disconnecting Peter,” joining previously announced star Chad Michael Murray in the upcoming family drama. The film is written and directed by Christopher Beatty.

	Hall will play Elizabeth Ruck, wife to Murray’s Peter Ruck, a woman working to hold her family together as her husband’s destructive patterns threaten to unravel them. The film follows the Ruck family as they reckon with the fallout of a past tragedy, and the question of whether to confront their pain or let it break them apart.
	

	Hall is a stage and screen veteran. She won a Tony for her performance in “Hedwig and the Angry Inch,”and is starring in Apple TVs “Your Friends & Neighbors.” She was also a cast member on “Snowpiercer.” Her films include “Becks,” “The Graduates” and “Honey Don’t!” She appeared in the original Broadway production of “Kinky Boots.”


	Eddie Micallef and Benjamin J. Murray will produce “Disconnecting Peter.” Thomas J. Molica is executive producing. Stephanie Holbrook is overseeing casting.

	“Lena has this rare ability to carry devastation and resolve in the same moment — that’s Elizabeth. She and Chad are going to bring something really special to this family,” Beatty said.

	Murray is known for “Sullivan’s Crossing,” “A Cinderella Story,” “Agent Carter,” “Freaky Friday” and “The Merry Gentlemen.” He first broke out on “One Tree Hill” and “Gilmore Girls.” He most recently appeared in last summer’s hit sequel, “Freakier Friday.” 

	Production on “Disconnecting Peter” is slated to begin in January 2027 in New Jersey, with additional casting underway.

schema.headline: ‘Your Friends & Neighbors’ Star Lena Hall Joins Chad Michael Murray in ‘Disconnecting Peter’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Magic: The Gathering Reveals New ‘The Hobbit’ Card Featuring Iconic J.R.R. Tolkien Character (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Magic: The Gathering will travel back to Middle-earth this month with the release of a new set of tabletop gaming cards based on J.R.R. Tolkien’s wo
body:
Magic: The Gathering will travel back to Middle-earth this month with the release of a new set of tabletop gaming cards based on J.R.R. Tolkien’s work. Variety has the exclusive first look at a card from the collection featuring a key character in the plot against the dragon Smaug.

	Releasing Aug. 14, “The Hobbit” set will feature cards “from the time-honored tale, blending rich storytelling with strategic play as players adventure alongside familiar friends and formidable foes,” including the gold Smaug the Magnificent headliner card, Middle-earth classic artist cards, and Dwarven language cards.
	

	Per the description for the set, “Journey from the Shire to the Lonely Mountain alongside Bilbo Baggins in a set that captures the whimsy and heart of one of fantasy’s most beloved adventures. Players will encounter trolls, ponder riddles in the dark, and come face-to-face with Smaug himself—brought to life through Magic’s gameplay and design.”


	Variety has an exclusive look at two variants of one new card from “The Hobbit” set, titled “Glóin the Mighty.” In this card, the “dwarf warrior” Glóin is seen battling with an goblin during an iconic scene from the book where he and Thorin Oakenshield’s defend their dwarf brethren and Bilbo on their journey. Glóin goes on to be the father of Gimli, one of Frodo’s fellowship members, in “The Lord of the Rings.”

	“The Hobbit” set is part of Magic’s “Universes Beyond” collection, which adds in third-party IP to the popular tabletop trading card game. Magic previously released a “The Lord of the Rings” set in June 2023 and took inspiration from those cards to continue the adaptation work with “The Hobbit” collection.
	

	Earlier this month, Magic: The Gathering maker Wizards of the Coast announced plans for its 2027 sets, which will include three mainline Magic sets and a trio of unannounced Universes Beyond collections done in collaboration with outside IP, like “The Hobbit.” 

	The subjects of those UB collections have not been revealed, but Wizards has confirmed the sets will be releasing in April, August and November of next year. Additionally, Magic will release three mainline sets that start a new story arc within MTG’s own universe, including “Nauctis: The Sunken Realm” (releasing in February 2027), “Kamigawa: Titanbreach” (June 2027), and “Zhalfir” (October 2027).

	See below for Variety‘s exclusive first look at two variants of the “Glóin the Mighty” cards from the upcoming “The Hobbit” Magic: The Gathering set.



	

					Wizards of the Coast

title: Why Canceling My Tour Relaunched and Revived My Career As an Independent Artist, by JP Saxe (Guest Column)
description: JP Saxe is a Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter. Last year, he made headlines after scheduling an ambitious headlining tour that he ended up canceli
body:
JP Saxe is a Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter. Last year, he made headlines after scheduling an ambitious headlining tour that he ended up canceling. Instead of making excuses, like many musicians in the same position have, Saxe got brutally honest about why he scrapped the dates, posting a TikTok and writing a guest column for Variety explaining how low ticket sales were to blame. Somehow, in a situation where his pride could have been irreparably harmed, Saxe felt empowered to soldier on, using the experience as a launching pad into the next phase of his career.
	

	Since then, he’s performed with the Jonas Brothers and contributed songwriting to Nick Jonas’ 2026 album “Sunday Best.” He picked back up on the live circuit, serving as direct support for Megan Moroney’s current sold-out arena tour. And, most notably, he’s gone independent after spending six years and releasing two albums on Arista Records. Most recently, he kickstarted his new era with the single “When I Lose You” in preparation for his forthcoming album “Okay Piano Guy,” out October 23. Below, Saxe discusses how he’s evolved since his tour cancellation and why it’s helped him look past the clutter surrounding what it means to be an artist.


	A year ago I wrote about canceling my tour. I wrote about it because I didn’t know what else to do besides tell the truth. It wasn’t strategic. It wasn’t meant to be seen as brave (as it was bizarrely labeled). It just felt less exhausting than pretending.

	I’ve resisted writing this “one-year-later” follow-up because I don’t want to act like that experience predicated a comeback story. The honesty of the first essay can’t depend on things having gone well afterward. It had to be worth telling even if nothing improved.
	

	And not everything has. But the cancellation did interrupt my life in ways I’m still trying to understand. I wouldn’t have made this album if I’d gone on that tour. I probably wouldn’t have started a production company with my band. I wouldn’t have spent the last year writing with so many artists I admire. I wouldn’t have become a Jonas cousin. Most importantly, I’m not sure I would’ve become an independent artist.

	In October, I’m releasing “Okay Piano Guy,” my first album as an independent artist. It’s the proudest I’ve ever been of a body of work. Not just because the songs belong to me in every way possible, but because the version of success I’m pursuing belongs to me too.

	That has not always been true.

	After “If the World Was Ending,” I set a trajectory for myself. Every next step had to be a step up. Every room had to be bigger than the last one. Every song had to reach more people. The line was supposed to keep moving in one direction, and my job was to make sure it never looked (to myself or anyone else) like I was moving backward.

	Since opening for him in 2019, I’d been pacing myself against Noah Kahan. A couple years later, I was playing the same venues he had played. It gave me a comforting little equation for my career. I could look at where he’d been, look at where I was, and imagine I was a few steps behind him on the same path.

	Then he became one of the biggest artists in the world. Which is wonderful. He deserves every bit of it. It also meant I needed to find a new person to measure myself against. So I did. Then someone else. Then someone else. I kept moving the finish line to wherever another artist happened to be standing.

	That fucked me up. A little bit because the comparisons made me jealous, but jealousy alone would’ve been simpler. Mostly, it just had me confused. I stopped knowing which ambitions were mine and which ones I’d adopted because they seemed like the appropriate next step for someone in my position.

	My ideas of success never lasted as long as it took me to achieve them. By the time I got somewhere I’d wanted to go, I was already looking ahead at someone who’d gone farther. The thing I’d worked toward felt insufficient before I’d even had the chance to enjoy it.
	

	I wasn’t building a career around what made my life feel meaningful. I was trying to maintain a trajectory.

	The canceled tour was the first undeniable break in that line. At the time, it felt like proof that I’d failed to keep pace. Now I think losing the trajectory may have been the only way I could start asking where I actually wanted to go.

	When I canceled the tour, the thing I was most afraid of wasn’t only losing the tour. It was losing the appearance of momentum. I had spent years learning that success needed to look continuous, public, and undeniable. Admitting that something hadn’t worked felt more dangerous than the failure itself.

	James Blake posted recently about how nearly every visible signal of success in music can now be manipulated. It’s a dope post. I highly recommend it and I think he’s right. When numbers, reactions, and entire narratives can be manufactured, protecting the appearance of success starts to feel like a waste of a creative life. Making people care has become a different art form than making something worth caring about.

	The more distance I got from the career trajectory I’d set for myself seven years ago, the more I realized I’d been measuring success using someone else’s definition.

	A disclaimer on this next thought: I don’t think record labels are inherently bad. I certainly didn’t think so when one helped get me out of sleeping in my car as a broke 25-year-old. I’ve worked with incredible people at labels. People who believed in me, fought for me, and genuinely changed my life.

	But I think a lot of artists (including me) make a counterintuitive mistake. We sign to a label because we trust people. In reality, we’re not signing to the people; we’re signing with a corporation. We can have an executive who understands our music better than anyone, who champions every idea we have, who goes to war for us in every meeting. And then they’re gone next week. Not because they stopped believing in us. Because people leave. They get promoted, they get fired. Leadership changes. Strategies change. Budgets change.

	Our relationship may have been with a person. But our contract was always with a corporation. And corporations and artists don’t wake up trying to accomplish the same thing.
	

	A label is focused on building the biggest business possible. Labels invest capital and hope enough artists become enormously successful to justify all the ones who don’t. Success, by necessity, becomes scale. Bigger records. Bigger numbers. None of that is evil. It’s math.

	An artist’s job is different. An artist isn’t trying to maximize a portfolio. An artist is trying to maximize a creative life. Sometimes those things overlap beautifully. Sometimes they don’t.

	A label benefits from momentum. An artist benefits from meaning. A label needs consistency. An artist sometimes needs to disappear for a year and come back with something earnest. A label wants certainty because certainty is easier to finance.

	Great art has never required certainty.

	Somewhere along the way, I confused the scorecard designed to evaluate a business with the scorecard I’d use to evaluate my own life. There are quieter ways the industry shapes us, too. Why does Spotify show us how many times every song has been streamed before we even press play? It’s become such a normal part of the experience that we rarely stop to question it. But why is that information there at all? Who does it actually serve? It certainly doesn’t help the song.

	After seeing those numbers every day, it’s hard not to let them become part of the way you measure yourself. We don’t just listen to songs anymore. We listen to songs while being reminded how everyone else has listened to them. Whether intentional or not, it’s a product decision that turns music into a public scoreboard and quietly monetizes artists’ insecurities. 

	Are we going to tell people to listen where they’ll simply listen, or where they’ll listen and make the number go up?

	I was chasing a version of success while slowly losing myself to the work required to maintain it. Then I canceled a tour. That decision didn’t fix my career. It didn’t reveal some perfect new path. But it did change the metric. More than anything, it showed me something I hadn’t expected. My community was far more excited to rally around the honesty of failure than the façade of success.

	“Okay Piano Guy” wouldn’t exist without that cancellation. Neither would the creative life around it. That doesn’t make the cancellation secretly good. I’m not interested in pretending every painful thing happens for a reason just because I eventually found a use for it. I don’t think independence is morally superior. I don’t suddenly know the “right” way to build a career.
	

	I just know that for the first time in a long time, I recognize myself in the ambitions I’m chasing. And whatever success looks like from here, at least I know whose definition I’m using.

schema.headline: Why Canceling My Tour Relaunched and Revived My Career As an Independent Artist, by JP Saxe (Guest Column)

title: Josh Hartnett Battles a Sea Monster in First Teaser for Netflix Thriller Series ‘Below’
description:
Netflix has released the first spinge-tingling teaser trailer for the thriller series “Below.” 

	In the teaser for the six-episode series, which ca
body:
Netflix has released the first spinge-tingling teaser trailer for the thriller series “Below.” 

	In the teaser for the six-episode series, which can be seen in its entirety below, a small seaside town is terrorized by a mysterious sea creature. “Below” will have its world premiere as part of the Primetime program at TIFF 2026 on Sept. 10 before its debut on Netflix on Oct. 8. 

	Josh Hartnett stars along with Charlie Heaton, Mackenzie Davis, Ruby Stokes, Kaleb Horn, Rohan Campbell, and Willow Kean. 
	

	The official description of the series states: 


	“Calvin Penney (Hartnett) is a big‑hearted but stubborn fisherman living in a small Newfoundland town, who’s still haunted by his father’s mysterious death from decades ago. When an unidentified sea creature begins terrorizing his hometown, Calvin must fight to hold his close-knit community together. Determined to keep his son Wade (Heaton) and the rest of his family safe, he teams up with a visiting marine researcher (Davis) to confront the creature and reveal the island’s buried secrets before it’s too late.” 

	The show was originally announced in February 2025, with Hartnett officially joining the series not long after. He previously starred in shows like “Penny Dreadful,” “Die Hart,” and “Paradise Lost.” 

	“Below” hails from creator, showrunner, and executive producer Jesse McKeown. Hartnett is an executive producer in addition to starring. Jessica Rhoades executive produces via Pacesetter, with Chris Hatcher, Jamie Childs, Louise Sutton, and Sharon Hall also executive producing. The series was filmed on location in St. John’s, Newfoundland, Canada.

schema.headline: Josh Hartnett Battles a Sea Monster in First Teaser for Netflix Thriller Series ‘Below’

title: Rick Moranis Ended Acting Retirement After Nearly 30 Years and Says ‘It Was Very Strange’ on ‘Spaceballs 2’ Set: ‘I Felt Like I Was in a Time Warp’
description:
Jul 28, 2026 8:35am PT	
	

	
		Rick Moranis Ended Acting Retirement After Nearly 30 Years and Says ‘It Was Very Strange’ on ‘Spaceball
body:
Jul 28, 2026 8:35am PT	
	

	
		Rick Moranis Ended Acting Retirement After Nearly 30 Years and Says ‘It Was Very Strange’ on ‘Spaceballs 2’ Set: ‘I Felt Like I Was in a Time Warp’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Michael Buckner/Variety
	

		
	
				
	Rick Moranis spent nearly 30 years retired from acting, but the comedy icon finally got back in front of the camera last fall to reprise the role of Lord Dark Helmet in “Spaceballs 2: The New One.” Acting again threw Moranis for a loop, not least because he was returning alongside his original “Spaceballs” co-stars to film a sequel nearly 40 years later.

	“Well, I kept having to pinch myself because I would look at Daphne [Zuniga] and Bill [Pullman] and George Wyner. And then there were all these young people,” Moranis said at Comic-Con (via People). “And I realized I was their age 39 years ago when we made this. And here we are now and my kids are the age of this.”Moranis added, “I felt like I was in a time warp, but I was in that outfit and wearing the helmet. And it just felt very strange to be honest with you. But it started to feel really good and I really started to love it.”
	

	“Spaceballs 2” reunites Moranis with original stars George Wyner as Colonel Sandurz, Daphne Zuniga as Princess Vespa, Bill Pullman as Lone Starr and Mel Brooks as Yogurt. Franchise newcomers include Josh Gad, Keke Palmer, Lewis Pullman and Anthony Carrigan, whose roles remain under wraps for now. “Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar” and “Will & Harper” helmer Josh Greenbaum directed the sequel. Gad co-wrote the script with Benji Samit and Dan Hernandez.


	Moranis’ last live-action role in a feature film was in the 1997 comedy sequel “Honey, We Shrunk Ourselves,” although he had voice roles in two “Brother Bear” movies in the mid-2000s. His acting work in the 21st century has largely been relegated to voice roles, including two seasons of the Canadian animated sitcom he co-created titled “Bob & Doug.”

	“Spaceballs: The New One” will release in theaters on April 23, 2027.
	


	
		More from Variety

schema.headline: Rick Moranis Ended Acting Retirement After Nearly 30 Years and Says ‘It Was Very Strange’ on ‘Spaceballs 2’ Set: ‘I Felt Like I Was in a Time Warp’

title: FiGa Films Snags Worldwide Rights to Guatemalan Drama ‘Nosotros’ Ahead of TIFF Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Boutique sales agency FiGa Films has pounced on the worldwide sales rights to Guatemalan drama “Nosotros” (meaning “Us”) ahead of its world premiere
body:
Boutique sales agency FiGa Films has pounced on the worldwide sales rights to Guatemalan drama “Nosotros” (meaning “Us”) ahead of its world premiere at the 51st Toronto Intl. Film Festival (TIFF).

	Playing at TIFF’s Discovery sidebar, “Nosotros” is written and directed by Joaquín Ruano, who said: “As this is my debut feature, it was essential to partner with a sales team that can guide the film through industry terrains I haven’t traveled before.”
	

	“I see the FiGa team as close collaborators across every stage of this process and I deeply value their proven track record championing Central American filmmakers I admire,” he added.


	Set amid a highly conservative Guatemalan society and its deep social inequalities, “Nosotros” follows a quiet, forbidden connection that emerges in an unlikely place, challenging the forces of prejudice, power and violence that surround it. Featuring Lola Vásquez, Jozef Coxaj and Mayra Salvador, the drama presents an intimate portrait of longing and survival.

	Romero (Coxaj) leaves his wife and son behind in the Guatemalan highlands to work as a private security guard in the capital, hoping for a different future. Immersed in an unforgiving culture of surveillance and machismo, his life takes an unexpected turn when he meets Nubia (Vásquez), a trans woman who owns a small shop in the mall he patrols.

	As their bond deepens, the two carve out a fleeting sense of safety and intimacy. But mounting fear and suspicion among Romero’s fellow guards soon threaten to destroy the fragile sanctuary they have found in one another.
	

	Ruano is among the rising talent from the small but increasingly prolific Central American region that continues to gain recognition at major festivals.

	A Guatemala-Mexico co-production, “Nosotros” is produced by Pamela Guinea (“Gasolina,” “Our Mothers”) and Ruano (“Roza”) via their production companies Cine Concepción and Cine Murciélago. Sandro Fiorin, CEO of FiGa Films, negotiated the pact with them.

	“My partnership with producer Pamela Guinea goes back more than 20 years to when we first met at San Sebastián,” said Fiorin. “Having collaborated on four films since then, working together on ‘Nosotros’ feels like a true family affair built on a rare level of industry trust and chemistry. We have actually been tracking this project since its early development at BrLab in 2016, and always knew it belonged on the FiGa slate. Its brilliant intersection of a tender, intimate love story and gripping social realism is exactly the kind of bold, urgent cinema that defines our brand.”“FiGa has been a fundamental partner in my career, having worked together across four very different films,” Guinea noted. “They bring a unique perspective and a genuine commitment to the cinema of our region, and I know that the international journey beginning for ‘Nosotros’ is in good hands.”

	Founded in 2006, FiGa Films is also a production and distribution company, with a library of over 80 films by both established and novice filmmakers, mainly from across Latin America.

	Some notable titles in its slate include “About Thirty” by Martín Shanly, “The Padilla Affair” by Pavel Giroud, “The Visitor” by Martín Boulocq, “Los Lobos” by Samuel Kishi Leopo, “Nudo Mixteco” by Ángeles Cruz and Panama’s “Beloved Tropic” by Ana Endara.

	The 51st TIFF runs over Sept. 10-20.

schema.headline: FiGa Films Snags Worldwide Rights to Guatemalan Drama ‘Nosotros’ Ahead of TIFF Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Tony Gilroy, Pedro Pascal’s ‘Behemoth!’ to World Premiere as NYFF Centerpiece Selection
description:
Film at Lincoln Center has named Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” as the centerpiece selection of the 64th New York Film Festival. 

	The film will have it
body:
Film at Lincoln Center has named Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” as the centerpiece selection of the 64th New York Film Festival. 

	The film will have its world premiere at Alice Tully Hall on Friday, Oct. 2, with Gilroy, its star Pedro Pascal, and additional members of the cast in attendance. Presented by Film at Lincoln Center in partnership with Rolex, the 64th New York Film Festival (NYFF64) will take place from Sept. 25 through Oct. 12.
	

	Pascal stars as Alex, a cellist picking up the pieces of a fractured life. A former child prodigy living in the shadow of a storied musical family, Alex has left his position with an orchestra in Chicago after fleeing a soured relationship with a manic ex (Olivia Wilde) and returns to Los Angeles to record Hollywood film scores and resolve unfinished family business. “Behemoth!” features a supporting cast that includes Eva Victor, Alexa Swinton, Kaya Ralls, Erik Griffin, JoBeth Williams and Margarita Levieva, with Hank Azaria and Will Arnett. It’s a Searchlight Pictures release.


	Gilroy wrote and directed the Oscar-winning “Michael Clayton” and created the Emmy-winning “Andor.” He also wrote the first three “Bourne” films and co-wrote “Rogue One: A Star Wars Story.”

	“I have been orbiting NYFF for the great majority of my life,” said Gilroy. “I was baptized by ‘Fitzcarraldo.’ I was tending bar across the street and a customer tipped me a single ticket. It was a bad seat to the most remarkable screening I’d ever attended. There were many memorable nights to follow. The Centerpiece invitation is a fantasy I’ve conjured more times than I care to admit. NYFF has always been the benchmark for me; the opportunity to premiere a film I cannot wait to show, in that hall, to that audience, feels every bit as thrilling as I’d imagined. I’m honored.”
	

	“We are delighted to present the world premiere of Tony Gilroy’s anticipated return to the big screen as this year’s NYFF Centerpiece,” said Dennis Lim, NYFF artistic director. “There is so much to savor in this immaculately crafted film, from its creative use of music to its note-perfect ensemble cast. Holding it all together is a tour de force by Pedro Pascal, one of the performances of the year from one of our true movie stars.”

schema.headline: Tony Gilroy, Pedro Pascal’s ‘Behemoth!’ to World Premiere as NYFF Centerpiece Selection

            The 2025 murder of Chrisean Rock's ex-boyfriend Karon "Ronny Doe" Cann remains unsolved ... but police tell TMZ the investigation is still active as detectives continue working to identify and catch the killer.
      
    
            Justin Mulcahy, a rep for the Anne Arundel County Police Department in Maryland, told us Monday night ... "We can confirm that it is an open and active investigation; however, we are unable to provide any additional details."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Before his death, Karon publicly claimed he was the father of Chrisean's son, Chrisean, Jr.
      
    
            She has always insisted Blueface was the father, despite the rapper denying the allegations.
      

            About a month later, Karon reportedly got in Chrisean's face at a mall while she was with her infant son, and cops were called.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In February 2025, Karon was shot and killed in Severn, Maryland, in what investigators believe was a targeted attack. 
      
    
            Cops rushed to a home in the Baltimore suburb after reports of a shooting and found Karon outside with multiple gunshot wounds. Paramedics treated him at the scene before taking him to a nearby hospital, where he later died.
      
    
            More than a year later, police still haven't publicly identified a suspect or person of interest, and the case remains unsolved.

            "The Young and the Restless" alum Brenda Dickson had some major drama in real life recently ... because she got tossed in the clink for battery ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Brenda -- who played Jill Foster Abbott on the famous soap opera -- was arrested and booked on July 9 for misdemeanor battery on a person, according to the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Office. She was released that same day on her own recognizance.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Law enforcement sources tell TMZ ... LAPD officers were called to a location in Hollywood on the night of July 8 for a battery investigation.
      

            Our sources say cops were told Brenda allegedly assaulted someone ... and, as a result, she was arrested. 
      
    
            It's unclear who the alleged victim was, what their relationship was to Brenda or what precipitated the alleged battery.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Brenda appeared on 'Young and the Restless' from 1973 to 1980 and from 1983 to 1987 ... and she also had cameos in "Men at Law," "The FBI," "Love, American Style," "Here We Go Again," and "Falcon Crest."
      
    
            We reached out to Brenda ... so far, no word back.

            He's starring in daily educational videos that each cover 1 year of U.S. history, according to the program's website.
      
    
            Because who better to educate America's youth than the actor behind a fictional TV doctor?
